analysis.one_liner: Expands Medicare preventive and mental health coverage, blocks a scheduled doctor pay cut, and restricts private plan marketing.
analysis.headline: Congress passed this Medicare overhaul over President Bush's veto — the House 383-41 and the Senate 70-26 on July 15, 2008 — after Senate Republicans first blocked it 58-40 in June.
analysis.plain_summary: This law improves Medicare for older and disabled Americans: it adds coverage for preventive services, gradually wipes out the higher copayments charged for outpatient mental health care by 2014, blocks a scheduled cut in doctors' Medicare pay and replaces it with a small increase through 2009, and expands help for low-income beneficiaries. It also bans aggressive sales tactics by private Medicare Advantage and drug plans — no gifts, cold calls, or cross-selling of annuities at sales pitches — and delays a program that would have forced competitive bidding on medical equipment suppliers. The cost is covered in part by trimming payments to private plans, labs, and dialysis providers.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries gain preventive coverage, steadily lower mental health copayments through 2014, more help enrolling in low-income programs, and continued access to doctors whose pay was facing a scheduled cut. Rural beneficiaries and veterans get grant-funded services; people with kidney disease get education coverage and cardiac and pulmonary rehabilitation become covered. Doctors, rural hospitals, ambulances, and pharmacies keep or gain Medicare payments.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Older and disabled Americans on Medicare

how_it_helps.text: Adds coverage of additional preventive services, including body mass index screening and end-of-life planning in the annual wellness visit [S3].
Phases out by 2014 the rule that counted only 50% of outpatient psychiatric expenses toward Medicare coverage, and raises payments for psychotherapy services by 5% through 2009 [S3].
Replaces a scheduled physician payment reduction with an increase for the second half of 2008 and 2009, keeping doctors from exiting Medicare [S3].

Bans Medicare Advantage and drug plan marketers from unsolicited contact, cross-selling products like annuities and life insurance, and providing meals at sales events, and requires licensed agents and state oversight [S3].

Extends programs that pay Medicare premiums and drug costs for low-income beneficiaries, waives their late-enrollment penalties, ends estate recovery of Medicare cost-sharing help, and funds Social Security and community assistance with enrollment [S3].

Extends rural hospital and ambulance payment programs, adds coverage of cardiac and pulmonary rehabilitation, kidney disease education, and barriers to telehealth, and adds grants for mental health services to rural veterans [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The cost falls partly on private Medicare Advantage insurers (reduced stabilization funding and stricter marketing rules), clinical laboratories (a fee-schedule update reduction from 2009 to 2013), and dialysis providers (reduced payment updates ahead of a bundled payment system). Taxpayers fund new grant programs, and the doctor-pay fix is only temporary, returning the payment problem to future Congresses.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private Medicare plans, labs, dialysis providers, taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The physician payment increase runs only through 2009, leaving the underlying Medicare doctor-payment formula unsolved and setting up the same crisis again the next year [S3].

Delaying full implementation of competitive bidding for medical equipment until after 2011 and requiring ongoing rental payments for oxygen equipment preserves higher payments to suppliers at federal expense [S3].
The bill pays for part of itself by reducing the update to clinical laboratory fees from 2009 through 2013 and cutting dialysis payment updates, costs some providers passed along or absorbed [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains for beneficiaries are broad and concrete: new preventive coverage, the end of the mental health copayment penalty, stronger low-income assistance, and a doctor-pay cut averted. The offsets are modest trims to labs, dialysis, and private plans, but the equipment-bidding delay is the weak point — it preserves payments to suppliers that the bidding program was designed to lower. The biggest honest criticism is that the doctor-payment fix is another one-year patch rather than a real solution, so the same fight had to be repeated.

outcome.mechanism: Both chambers passed it, President Bush vetoed it, and large bipartisan majorities in the House and Senate overrode the veto the same day, making it Public Law 110-275.

narrative.text: The House passed the bill 355-59 on June 24, 2008, under a fast-track procedure requiring a two-thirds vote; 226 of 235 Democrats and 129 of 199 Republicans voted yes [S8][S9].
On June 26 Senate Republicans blocked the first procedural vote — 58 senators voted to move forward, short of the 60 needed — stopping the bill despite nearly every Democrat supporting it [S8][S10].
After the July 4 recess, supporters revived the bill: on July 9 the Senate voted 69-30 to move forward, with 18 Republicans switching to yes, and then passed the bill without change [S8][S11].
President Bush vetoed the bill on July 15, 2008 [S8].

The same day, the House overrode the veto 383-41 (all voting Democrats plus 153 Republicans) and the Senate overrode it 70-26 (all voting Democrats plus 21 Republicans), and the bill became Public Law 110-275 [S8][S12][S13].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare beneficiaries, physicians, rural hospitals, and pharmacies came out ahead — the law delivered new coverage and averted a doctor pay cut. Medical equipment suppliers also gained, since the law delayed the competitive bidding program that would have cut their payments.

sides.party_line_note: Opposition came almost entirely from Republicans — 39 of 49 Senate Republicans blocked the first procedural vote and 59 House Republicans voted no — but the final votes were bipartisan: 153 of 199 House Republicans and 21 of 49 Senate Republicans joined every voting Democrat to override the veto.

industries.note: The law cancels a scheduled Medicare pay cut and raises the update through 2009, plus incentives for electronic prescribing. Patients benefit because doctors are less likely to stop taking Medicare patients.

The law delays full competitive bidding until after 2011 and requires Medicare to keep paying rental for oxygen equipment indefinitely, locking in supplier revenue that the bidding program was designed to reduce.

industries.industry: Medicare Advantage and drug plan insurers
industries.note: They lose their freedom to use gifts, cold calls, and cross-selling of annuities at sales events, and face reduced stabilization funding, but they keep their central role in Medicare. The restrictions were aimed at protecting seniors from misleading sales tactics.
A fee-schedule update reduction from 2009 through 2013 helps finance the bill's beneficiary improvements, a cost that could reach patients through lab access if providers cut back.
Payment updates are reduced and a bundled payment system with quality incentives begins in 2011, trimming revenue while tying it to quality measures.
Drug plans must pay clean claims promptly with interest on late payments, and long-term care pharmacies get 30-90 days to submit claims, improving pharmacy cash flow and access.

Extended rural hospital grants, sole community hospital payment rebasing, ambulance payment extensions, and grants for veterans' mental health services support care in areas where residents have few alternatives.
